summary:
Cabo Verde does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Article 71 of the 1886 Penal Code had prohibited unnatural acts; a 2004 amendment removed all provisions relating to consensual homosexual sex, making Cabo Verde the second country on its continent to decriminalise after South Africa. The age of consent stood at 16 at decriminalisation, the same as for consensual heterosexual acts, and was 14 as of 2015.

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. Civil law blocked the change to a female legal name sought by Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed transgender woman in Cabo Verde, who came out in 1997 at age 19 and in a local newspaper in 1998; an interview published 22 June 2016 records that no route to a legal gender change existed then, and no later statute or administrative procedure appears in the sources. A visitor whose passport marker differs from presentation should expect no local precedent for documentary flexibility.

Workplace protection stops at sexual orientation. Articles 45(2) and 406(3) of the Labour Code, in force since 2008, ban discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation, with a fine set case by case, and article 406(3) applies the same penalty to unlawful dismissal on those grounds. An international LGBTI rights organisation's profile, updated 12 March 2026, records that the protection does not extend to gender identity, so a trans worker has no statutory basis for a discrimination or dismissal claim on that ground.

No same-sex union is recognised. On 11 July 2017 Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva stated that legalising same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, a position taken after community demands for civil unions and marriage. A trans visitor in a relationship read as same-sex under birth-sex status should expect no recognition of that partnership locally.

Violence documented against trans people in these sources is limited and undated. Tchinda Andrade reported verbal violence and two physical attacks in the interview of 22 June 2016, which gives no dates for those incidents, and no later instance is documented. The 2010 United States Department of State human rights report found that societal discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity continued to be a problem despite the legal provisions protecting homosexual conduct.

The state has committed internationally to protection on gender-identity grounds. On 18 December 2008 Cabo Verde joined 65 other states in a UN General Assembly statement affirming that human rights apply regardless of sexual orientation and gender identity, condemning killings, torture and arbitrary arrest on that basis, and urging an end to criminal penalties. It signed a 2011 UN document condemning violence and discrimination against LGBT people, made anti-discrimination commitments in its 2024 Universal Periodic Review, and on 28 June 2025 was the only African country to sign a 15-state foreign-ministers declaration rejecting criminalisation and stigmatisation based on sexual orientation and gender identity, supporting the eradication of transphobic harassment and socio-labour inclusion for trans people, and calling for an end to conversion practices. Cabo Verde is one of two African members of the UN LGBTI Core Group.

Civil society operates openly. LGBTIQ organisations register freely; the first Pride parade was held in Mindelo in June 2013, the first Praia Pride three years later, and the 2018 Pride Week in Praia combined a parade with campaigns by the Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, the Associação LGBTI de Praia and the Associação Arco Iris petitioning the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law, with the state gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women engaged. No LGBT organisation was active in the country in 2010 according to the US State Department report of that year.
tangentialFactors:
Public-attitude polling measures acceptance of gay and lesbian people, not of trans people. Outright International reports 2019–21 polls in which 82% of respondents would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour, and a 2020 Afrobarometer poll found 80% of Cape Verdeans would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour, one of only four African countries polled with a majority in favour. Afrobarometer Dispatch No. 362 of May 2020 places Cabo Verde, Namibia and São Tomé and Príncipe apart as particularly tolerant countries while finding that tolerance toward sexual minorities remains weak even among younger respondents. No source in this inventory reports a comparable measure of attitudes toward transgender people.

Cabo Verde has been described as one of the most tolerant countries in Africa toward gays and lesbians, and occasionally as the most tolerant on the continent for LGBT people, though the same sources report continuing societal discrimination. São Vicente is characterised as very welcoming to the LGBT community, and Tchinda Andrade described Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries and São Vicente as relaxed, in the same 2016 interview in which she reported the attacks.

Political alignment on partnership recognition is not uniform. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva's July 2017 statement distancing himself from opposition to same-sex marriage came after MpD secretary-general Miguel Monteiro had voiced opposition and after LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.
localsOnly:
Locals often refer to transgender people by a term derived from the name of Cabo Verde's first publicly self-outed trans woman, a usage recorded in the sources without any accompanying legal effect.

The Labour Code protection against workplace discrimination and discriminatory dismissal on grounds including sexual orientation, in force since 2008, is a resident-facing entitlement; it does not name gender identity. Cabo Verde is one of few African countries with such a statutory protection.

Organised advocacy is domestic and institutionalised. The Associação Gay de Cabo Verde was established by 2013 after a period in which no LGBT organisation was active, and the 2018 Praia Pride was organised with the state gender-equality institute ICIEG and the Praia Government, with petitions directed at the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and anti-discrimination legislation. LGBTIQ groups register without restriction.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses airport or border screening, document-marker flagging, anatomy inspection, segregated facilities, custody, or medical care for transgender visitors or residents. The Wikipedia article on LGBT rights in Cabo Verde supplies no statute, provision, penalty or procedure on legal gender recognition, marker changes, screening, facilities, custody or trans-specific healthcare, and the absence of such content is not evidence that no rule exists.

Whether any legal gender recognition procedure was enacted after the 2016 interview is unresolved here; the sources contain neither a permitting statute nor a documented refusal after that date.

The age of consent figure of 14 is stated as of 2015 and is not confirmed by a later source in this inventory.

The sources provide no trans-specific violence or killing statistics for Cabo Verde, no denominator and no general homicide rate, so no comparison of trans risk against background violence can be made from this material. The attacks reported by Tchinda Andrade are undated in the source, and no later incident is documented.

How a gender marker that differs from presentation would be treated at entry, in visa processing or in any identity check is not sourced.
